exp.0:6:
This verse continues a list of virtues that the believer should add to their faith. Two more are added here: brotherly love, which is sincere affection toward brothers and sisters in the faith, and charity, which in this verse means love, a love that seeks the good of the other even without receiving anything in return.

The one speaking is the apostle Peter, writing to believers who already had faith in Christ. He insists that true faith must grow and bear fruit. Peter wants them not to be idle or unfruitful, but to show a transformed life, remembering that God cleansed them from their past sins.

For today: do not be content with loving only those you happen to like. Ask God to help you take one concrete step this week, such as visiting, forgiving, or helping a brother or sister who is hard to love. In this way your love will grow toward a more genuine self-giving.
exp.0:7:
It says that if the qualities mentioned before (faith, virtue, knowledge, self-control, patience, godliness, brotherly affection and love) are present in us and keep growing, they will not leave us idle, that is, inactive or doing nothing, nor unproductive, meaning without fruit. Knowing Jesus Christ should produce a life that bears fruit.

The apostle Peter writes to believers and shows them that true faith must grow. It comes from his urging them to make every effort to add these qualities to their faith. Then he warns that whoever lacks them becomes spiritually blind and forgets that God forgave them.

Today we can choose one of those virtues, for example patience, and ask God for help to practice it this week at home or at work. In this way our knowledge of Christ shows in what we do.
exp.0:8:
He says that whoever lacks these qualities (faith, goodness, knowledge, self-control, patience, godliness, brotherly affection, and love) lives as if they were blind. Seeing only what is right in front of them, they do not look toward what lasts forever. They have forgotten that God cleansed them from their past sins. Love is the word for the last quality in the list.

Peter writes to believers, almost as a farewell, to remind them of what matters most before his death. He wants their faith to grow and not remain only in words. Forgetting what Christ has done leads to a life that bears no fruit. Many understand the person described to be a careless believer; others think that the person may never have truly believed. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: remind yourself each day that God has forgiven you. Thank him, and ask for help to grow in one specific quality, such as patience or love for your brothers and sisters.
exp.0:16:
This verse says that Jesus received honor and glory from God the Father. That happened when a voice came to him from the excellent glory, that is, from the majestic presence of God. The voice said: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."

The apostle Peter speaks here near the end of his life. He wants believers to remember what he taught. He tells them that his message is not based on invented stories, but on what he saw and heard himself. He refers to the moment on the holy mountain, which many understand to be the transfiguration of Jesus, according to the Gospels.

For today: our faith rests on a firm testimony. When you doubt, return to the Father's words about Jesus and listen to him with confidence.
exp.0:18:
This verse says that believers have the prophetic word, that is, God's messages in the Scriptures, and that it is very firm and sure. Peter encourages them to pay attention to it, like someone following a torch in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star (an image of Christ and his light) rises in their hearts. The phrase "until the day dawn" simply means until morning arrives.

The apostle Peter is speaking near the end of his life. He has just recalled seeing the glory of Jesus on the mountain and hearing the voice of the Father. Now he affirms that Scripture is an even firmer foundation. Some believe the "day" refers to the return of Christ; others, to an inner light that grows. Both ideas fit the text.

For today: when you feel confused or are in dark times, open the Bible each day, even for a few minutes, and let its light guide your next step.
exp.1:3:
The verse says that God did not spare the angels who sinned.

Peter writes to believers and warns them against false teachers who would take advantage of them out of greed. To show that the punishment of these deceivers is certain, he gives examples from the past: the angels, the flood, and Sodom. The verse does not say when or how those angels fell; some connect it with Genesis 6 and others with an earlier rebellion, and scholars do not agree.

For today: if God judged even such exalted beings, let us take his warning seriously. Let us beware of those who teach with pleasant words but seek their own gain, and let us live with reverence, trusting that God cares for his own.
exp.1:4:
God did not let the ancient world go unpunished, but judged the people who lived there before the flood. Yet he took care of Noah, who is called a preacher of righteousness, that is, someone who proclaimed what is right. Seven other people were saved with him, eight in all. The flood came upon a world of the ungodly, people who lived without reverence for God.

The apostle Peter writes to believers, warning them about false teachers who would exploit them with deceptive words. To show that God does judge, he gives examples: the angels who sinned, the flood, and Sodom and Gomorrah. In each case, God also rescued the righteous.

For today: do not be discouraged if living with integrity leaves you alone or in the minority. God sees those who are faithful to him, cares for them, and knows how to deliver them. Keep doing what is right, and with your life and your words bear witness, as Noah did.
exp.1:17:
This verse says that the false teachers speak with big, proud words that are empty. With them they lure in people who had only just escaped a life of error, the way bait draws in a fish. They promise to satisfy the desires of the body, and to live without restraint.

Peter, an apostle of Jesus, writes to believers to warn them against teachers who lead others astray. He speaks mainly to new Christians, who are the easiest to deceive. The verses that follow say that these teachers promise freedom, but they themselves are slaves to corruption.

For today: be wary of anyone who promises freedom without limits or who sounds very impressive, but pulls you away from a clean life. Compare what you hear with the Bible and with the character of Christ.
exp.1:21:
They say that what happened to those false teachers is what a true proverb describes: the dog goes back to eat what it threw up, and the sow, even though she was washed, goes back to rolling in the mud. "Mud" is the mud; "vomit" is what the dog brought back up; "sow" is the female pig. Peter quotes the first proverb from Proverbs 26:11, and the second seems to be a popular saying of his time.

The apostle Peter writes to warn believers about false teachers who had come to know Christ but returned to a life of sin, and who were leading others astray. Interpreters debate whether they were genuine believers who fell away or people who knew the truth only from the outside. Peter, in any case, makes it clear that turning back is very serious.

For today: do not see your past sin as something attractive. If God has cleansed you, guard your heart, stay close to Christ and to sincere brothers and sisters, and ask his help each day so that you do not return to the mud.
exp.2:3:
It says that some will mock by asking, "Where is the promise of his coming?" They argue that since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation. The word "fathers" here means the ancestors who have died.

Peter, an apostle of Jesus, writes to believers to warn them about mockers who will live according to their own desires. These people rely on the world seeming not to change. Peter reminds them of what the prophets and apostles said, and in the verses that follow he answers that God did act before, in the flood. So the fact that everything looks the same does not prove that God will not act.

When time passes and things stay the same, it is easy to doubt. Today we can remember that God's patience is not forgetfulness. Be encouraged to trust his Word, to live faithfully, and not to let yourself be swept along by mockery.
exp.2:6:
This verse says that the heavens and the earth we see today are not left on their own, but God sustains them by the same word through which he created everything. That same word also keeps them reserved for fire, for the day when God will judge. "Destruction" means ruin, and "ungodly" people are those who live without reverence for God.

The apostle Peter writes to believers who were hearing from mockers. They were saying that nothing changes and that God would not intervene. Peter reminds them that the world was already judged by the flood, so his word has power. The next verse clarifies that God is not slow, but patient, because he wants everyone to turn to repentance.

For today: do not take God's patience as permission to delay. If there is something you need to set right with him, do it today, and pray for someone close to you so that they too may return to God.
exp.2:9:
This verse says that the day of the Lord will come by surprise, like a thief who enters at night. On that day the heavens will pass away with a loud roar, that is, with a great noise. The basic components of the universe (though some think of the stars) will be dissolved by fire. The earth and the works done on it will be burned up, that is, tested and exposed.

Peter writes to believers who were hearing mockery from people who said Christ would never return. He reminds them that God is not late; He is patient and wants everyone to repent. Christians interpret in different ways whether he is speaking of total destruction or of a purification and renewal.

For today: since no one knows when that day will come, live with sincerity and gratitude, without putting off your reconciliation with God or with others. Spend your time on what lasts: loving, forgiving, and obeying.
exp.2:13:
Peter says that since believers look forward to new heavens and a new earth, they should work hard to live in such a way that God finds them without stain, blameless, and at peace with Him.

Peter writes to Christians and calls them "beloved" with the affection of a shepherd. He has just spoken of the day of the Lord, when the present world will be purified. Some were mocking that Christ was taking so long, and Peter wants the waiting to produce holiness, not carelessness. He then explains that the Lord's patience is an opportunity for salvation.

For today: if you are waiting for Christ's return, that hope should shape your daily decisions. Today you can examine an attitude or habit that takes away your peace with God or with others, confess it, and ask Him for help to change.
exp.2:14:
He says that we should see the patience of the Lord as an opportunity for salvation. If God is slow to return, it is not out of carelessness, but because he gives time for people to repent. Peter adds that Paul, his beloved brother, also wrote about this with the wisdom God gave him.

Peter writes to believers who faced mockery, since some said that Jesus would never return. Earlier, Peter explained that the Lord is not slow but patient, because he does not want anyone to perish (3:9). Here he mentions Paul with respect, without competing with him. It is not known with certainty which of Paul's letters he means, and scholars have debated this.

When you feel that God is slow, do not see it as indifference. Use that time to grow in faith, live in peace, and draw near to others with the message of Christ.
exp.2:15:
Peter says that Paul speaks of these things in almost all of his letters, and that there are points in them that are hard to understand. Some people are untaught, and others are unstable. These people twist those texts, meaning they bend them so that they say what they do not say, just as they do with the rest of the Scriptures. This leads them to their own ruin.

Peter writes near the end of his life to believers who are waiting for the return of Christ. He asks them to live in peace and holiness, and he sees the patience of the Lord as an opportunity for salvation. He mentions Paul with affection and places his letters alongside the other Scriptures. He warns them against deceptive teachers.

That something is hard does not mean we should abandon it. Read the Bible with humility, compare each passage with the rest of Scripture, ask help from the church, and do not use a single verse to justify what you already wanted to believe.
exp.0:0:
Peter introduces himself as a "servant," meaning someone who belongs to his Lord and obeys him, and as an "apostle," meaning someone sent out with authority by Jesus. He writes to those who have received a faith as precious as the apostles' own. This faith comes through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ, the one who is both God and Savior.

Peter writes this letter to believers, probably near the end of his life, to encourage them to grow and not to be led astray by false teachers. At the very start, he reminds them that their faith is not second-class. Some scholars debate exactly who he was addressing, but the message is meant for all believers.

Today, you do not need to feel less than other Christians because of your background or your experience. Your faith has the same value before God, because it rests on Christ and not on you. Rest in that, and grow with confidence.
exp.1:14:
They have left the straight path and wandered off, following the way of Balaam, son of Beor. Balaam "loved the wages of wickedness," that is, he wanted the gain or payment that came from doing evil.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians to warn them against false teachers who live in sin and greed. He compares them to Balaam, a prophet of the Old Testament (Numbers 22–24) who, according to the account, was tempted by the riches offered to him to curse Israel. Peter wants the church to recognize them and not follow them.

For today: examine your motives. Before you serve, teach, or decide anything, ask yourself whether you are seeking to please God or your own benefit. Ask Him to keep you faithful, even when doing what is right comes at a cost.
exp.2:17:
This verse says "grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ." Peter calls Jesus both Lord and Savior. "But" connects this verse with what Peter has just said before it. The final phrase, where Peter gives glory to Jesus, means "both now and to the day of eternity," that is, today and forever.

Peter wrote this letter near the end of his life, to believers who were facing false teachers. He warned them not to be led astray by error and lose their firm footing. His answer is not only "be careful," but "keep growing." Knowing Christ better is a strong protection. Some understand "grace" as the favor of God that we receive, and others also as the way of living that flows from that favor.

For today: set aside a fixed time each day to read the Gospels and get to know Jesus more closely. In this way your faith is strengthened and stays firm.
exp.2:10:
This verse asks a question: since everything will be destroyed in this way, what kind of people ought you to be? The instruction that follows is to conduct yourselves in holiness and godliness. Here "conduct" refers to the way a person lives, the whole of their behavior, and not only their speech. "Holiness" speaks of a life set apart for God, and "godliness" of a heart that honors and loves him.

Peter writes to believers who were being troubled by scoffers. They mocked the idea that Christ had not yet returned. Peter answers that God is patient and that the day of the Lord will surely come. So instead of arguing about dates, he calls them to live with seriousness and hope.

For today: do not cling to what passes away, such as money, success, or possessions. Ask yourself each day, "How can I live today in a way that pleases God?" Then take one concrete step, such as forgiving someone, being honest, or setting aside time to pray.
exp.2:1:
Peter wants believers to remember two things: what the holy prophets of the Old Testament foretold, and what the Lord commanded through the apostles. In this verse, "commanded" refers to the authoritative teaching that the apostles passed on on behalf of Jesus. "Lord and Savior" refers to Jesus.

Peter writes his second letter to Christians who are in danger of being led astray. In the verse that follows, he announces that mockers will come who will doubt the promise of Christ's return. For this reason he asks them to hold on to what they have already been taught. He joins the voice of the prophets with that of the apostles as one trustworthy message.

For today: when doubts or mockery about the faith arise, return to the Bible. Read it steadily and remember what God has already said, because recalling his word sustains you.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that the angels, although they have much greater strength and power than any human being, do not dare to bring slanderous charges against those they are speaking about before God. The word "yet" in the verse introduces this contrast, meaning "although" or "even so." Such a charge is abusive and insulting. Interpreters debate who these "they" are: they may be fallen angelic beings or spiritual authorities; the text does not fully clarify this.

Peter, an apostle of Jesus, writes to believers to warn them against arrogant false teachers. These men spoke with contempt about things they did not understand. Peter contrasts them with the angels, who, though more powerful, act with humility and leave judgment to God.

Today we can learn to speak with humility. Before we criticize or mock what we do not understand, let us remember that God is the just judge, and that we are called to prudence and respect.
exp.1:8:
This verse says that the Lord knows how to rescue the godly, that is, those who honor him and are faithful to him, when they go through trials. It also says that he holds the unrighteous, those who live without regard for what is right, for punishment on the day of judgment. Here the word "trials" refers to difficulties and hardships, not only a pull toward sin. The idea of punishment points to a just and deserved judgment.

The apostle Peter writes to believers who were facing false teachers who lived a corrupt life. Just before this verse, he gives examples from the past: God judged the wicked, but rescued Noah and Lot. Peter wants to show that God is not careless: he takes care of his own and does not let wickedness go unpunished forever.

Today, if you are surrounded by a difficult or unjust environment, do not lose heart. Keep doing what is right and pray with confidence, knowing that God sees everything, sustains you, and has the final word.
exp.1:13:
They say these false teachers have eyes full of adultery, meaning they look at people with impure desire and cannot stop sinning. "Seduce" means to lure or hook, the way one uses bait; they draw in people who are unsteady, that is, weak and unsure in their faith. Their hearts are trained in greed: practiced at wanting more and more. "Accursed children" describes those who live under judgment because of their way of life.

The apostle Peter writes to believers to warn them about false teachers who slip into the church, eat with them, and lead them astray through their bad example. His goal is to protect Christians so they will not be deceived. Peter moves right away to the example of Balaam, who loved money more than obeying God.

For today: take care what you look at and what you desire, and be wary of anyone who teaches while seeking their own gain. Stand firm in the Word and in a healthy church so that you do not become unsteady.
exp.0:5:
This verse continues a list of qualities that the believer is to add to their faith. "Knowledge" means understanding, the ability to grasp what God has revealed. "Self-control" is mastery over oneself, knowing how to control one's desires. "Perseverance" is holding firm through trials. "Reverence for God" is respect and awe toward Him, not a fear that paralyzes.

The apostle Peter writes near the end of his life to believers who already have faith in Christ. He reminds them that God gave them great promises and rescued them from the corruption of the world. Now he encourages them to work hard at growing, because true faith does not stand still but bears fruit in character.

For today: what you know of God should lead you to control yourself in small matters, such as your temper, your words, or your spending. Ask God for help this week to practice self-control in one specific situation, and do not give up if it is hard.
exp.2:0:
Peter calls the believers "beloved," meaning dear and loved. He tells them that this is his second letter to them, and that both letters are reminders meant to stir them toward wholesome thinking.

The one speaking is the apostle Peter, and he is writing near the end of his life. Many think the first letter is 1 Peter, though some scholars debate this. His purpose, according to the verses that follow, is that they remember the teachings of the prophets and the apostles, because scoffers would come, led by their own desires.

For today: it is not enough to have heard the truth once. We can set aside a steady time to reread the Bible and recall what God has already taught us, so that our minds stay firm in the face of mockery and doubt.
exp.1:9:
God's judgment is especially reserved for those who give in to the corrupt desires of the flesh and who look down on authority. He also speaks of people who are bold and self-willed, unafraid to slander glorious beings. The corrupt desires are disordered longings that lead people into impurity and sinful pleasures.

The apostle Peter is speaking. He warns believers about false teachers who slip into the church. Earlier he gave examples such as Noah and Lot, whom God rescued while judging the wicked. Peter wants the faithful to know that God takes care of his own and that the arrogant will not go unpunished.

Today we can examine our attitude: do we live with humility before God and respect authority, or do we act with pride and mockery? Let us ask God for a submissive and clean heart.
exp.0:14:
Peter says that he will work hard so that, after he has departed, believers will be able to recall these teachings at all times. "I will make every effort" means he will make a sincere and steady effort. "After my departure" refers to his death, and "to recall" means to remember.

Peter writes at the end of his life, and he knows his death is near, as Jesus had shown him. He speaks of his body as a "tent," a temporary dwelling. He wants to leave the church firmly grounded, so he insists on the truth of the gospel. Many think this letter works like his spiritual last will, and the verses that follow support this, since he was an eyewitness of the glory of Christ.

Today we can do the same: put in writing or tell others, especially the young, what God has done in our lives and what the Bible teaches. In this way the faith is not lost when we are no longer here.
exp.1:11:
Peter says that these false teachers speak against spiritual things they do not understand. He compares them to irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be captured and destroyed. A "creature of instinct" is one that acts on its natural drives rather than on reason. He says that, like such creatures, they too will be destroyed.

Peter, an apostle of Jesus, writes to believers to warn them about false teachers who slip into the church. These men live in wild indulgence, despise authority, and mock spiritual realities, even powers that not even angels dare to insult. Peter wants the church to recognize them and not be carried away by them.

Today, before we criticize or mock what we do not understand, it is wise to stop and act with humility. We can study the Bible, ask mature believers, and pray. In this way we avoid speaking with pride, and we also learn to tell apart those who teach with sincerity from those who only follow their own desires.
exp.2:7:
This passage says we should not overlook something important: with God, time does not work the way it does for us. With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day. The phrase "do not let this one thing escape your notice" is a call to pay close attention. "Beloved" is a loving way of addressing believers.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who were wondering why Jesus had not yet returned. Some were mocking that wait. Peter reminds them that God is faithful and that His timetable is not ours. The verses that follow explain that this delay is patience, since God wants everyone to repent. Many understand the phrase as a way of showing that God is not limited by time, not as a formula for calculating dates.

Today, when you feel that God is slow to answer or to fulfill what He has promised, trust that He works with wisdom and patience. While you wait, live with faith and hope.
exp.0:11:
Peter says he will always keep reminding them of these things, even though they already know them and are firm in the truth they now have, which is the gospel teaching they have received and live by.

The speaker is the apostle Peter, who is writing to believers and knows his life will end soon (vv. 13-14). He has just urged them to grow in faith, virtue, and love (vv. 5-11). That is why he insists: he wants them, once he is no longer with them, to remain firm and to remember what is essential.

For today: even if you already know the basic truths of the faith, do not stop reviewing them. Set aside regular time to read the Bible, return to what is essential, and encourage others to do the same. Remembering keeps us firm.
exp.2:16:
What it says: Peter calls the believers "beloved" and reminds them that they already know these things. He asks them to be on their guard so that they are not carried away by the error of lawless people. The word "lawless" describes those who live without regard for God's law or any restraint. If the believers became careless, they could lose their secure standing, that is, their stability in the faith.

Context: Peter writes this letter near the end of his life, to strengthen the churches. Earlier he spoke of false teachers who twist the Scriptures. Now he closes with a loving warning and with a way forward: growing in Christ.

For today: It is not enough to know that false teachings exist; we must actively guard ourselves. Read the Bible regularly, compare it with what you hear, and seek to grow every day in the grace and knowledge of Jesus. A faith that grows stays firm.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that Lot, a righteous man, lived among the people of Sodom. Day after day he saw and heard lawless deeds, and this tormented his soul. The word "tormented" in this verse means that he suffered and was troubled deep inside. The "lawless" people are those who live without regard for God or for others.

The apostle Peter writes to believers to warn them about false teachers. He gives examples from the past: God judged Sodom, but rescued Lot. In this way he shows them that God knows how to care for His own and also knows how to judge those who live in wickedness. The verse reminds us that Lot suffered because of what he saw, although the Bible in other passages also shows that he had his failures.

For today: if you live in an environment where wrongdoing has become normal, do not harden yourself. Ask God for a sensitive heart, stay firm in what is right, and trust that He cares for you and knows how to act with justice.
exp.2:8:
God is not slow in keeping what he promised, even though some people think he is. In truth, God is patient with us. He does not want anyone to be lost, but he wants everyone to turn their life around. Being lost means being destroyed or ruined, and turning one's life around means returning to God with a sincere heart.

Peter writes to believers who were facing mockers. These people laughed at the promise that Christ would return, because time kept passing and nothing seemed to happen. Peter answers that God measures time differently than we do, and that his apparent delay is an act of mercy. Some understand this as directed especially toward the believers, others toward all of humanity, but in both cases the patient heart of God is shown.

Today, when you feel that God is taking his time, trust that his waiting has a loving purpose. Use it to return to him and to pray for those who do not yet know him.
exp.1:19:
This verse says that if some people have escaped the corruption of the world through knowing our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and then become tangled up in it again and are overcome by it, their final condition is worse than their first. The "corruption" is the things that stain life; the "final condition" is where they end up; and the "first" is how they were when they started.

The apostle Peter warns against false teachers who promise freedom, yet they themselves are slaves to their vices. Peter shows how they deceive believers who have only just come out of error. Interpreters debate whether he is speaking of true believers who fall away or of people who knew the truth without fully giving themselves to it; the text itself does not completely settle the question.

For today: do not take lightly what Christ has already done for you. If you feel the pull to return to a habit that once enslaved you, do not stay alone; seek counsel, prayer, and firm friendships in the faith, and remember that Jesus does give true freedom.
exp.2:11:
Peter says that believers wait for and hurry toward the day of God, when the heavens will be destroyed by fire and the elements will melt in the heat. "Conduct" in the verse before means behavior or the way a person lives. "Elements" can refer to the components of the universe; it is understood in several ways.

The apostle Peter writes to believers who hear mockery from those who say that Christ will never return. He reminds them that God is patient and that his day will arrive unexpectedly. For this reason he calls them to live with seriousness and hope. Some think that "hurrying" means living in such a way that the day comes soon; others, that it means longing for it eagerly.

Today we can ask ourselves each morning: "How would I live today if I remembered that God holds everything in his hands?" That remembrance helps us forgive, speak the truth, and serve with peace, without clinging to what passes away.
exp.2:2:
In this verse, we are first told to understand something important: in the last days, scoffers will come, people who mock the faith. They follow their own evil desires. The phrase "last days" refers to the final times, and the desires mentioned are the wrong longings of the heart.

The apostle Peter writes his second letter to stir up believers and to remind them of what the prophets and the apostles said. He wants to prepare them for those who would make fun of the promise that Christ will come again. The verses that follow show their mockery: "Where is the promise of his coming?" Some understand "last days" to mean the whole time from Christ until his return.

For today: if someone mocks your faith, do not be surprised or discouraged. Return to the Word of God, pray, and stand firm, waiting with patience and obeying Christ.
exp.1:2:
This verse says that false teachers, driven by greed, will take advantage of believers to profit from them, using deceptive words. The phrase "exploit you" means treating people as a means to gain. Peter adds that the long-standing verdict against these teachers remains in force, and their destruction does not sleep.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians to warn them that, just as there were false prophets in Israel, false teachers will also arise among them. He wants them to be alert and to know that God does not ignore deception. The examples that follow, such as the fallen angels and the flood, show that God does judge.

Today we can examine carefully what we are taught. If a teacher seems more interested in your money than in your growth, compare his words with the Bible and pray for discernment. Trust that God cares for his people and will do justice.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that God judged the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah and brought them to destruction, reducing them to ashes. Their fate stands as an example for those who would later live without fear of God or regard for Him. The phrase "reducing them to ashes" describes complete ruin, and the wording points to a warning that the same kind of judgment is coming on the ungodly.

The apostle Peter writes to believers who were facing false teachers. To warn them, he gives three examples of judgment: the angels who sinned, the flood in the time of Noah, and Sodom and Gomorrah. With the next verse, he shows that God also rescued Lot, the righteous man. In this way he teaches that God judges sin, but cares for those who are faithful to him.

For today: do not take lightly the kindness of God. Live with respect toward Him, and if you find yourself surrounded by an environment that turns away from God, trust that He sees your faithfulness and knows how to sustain you.
exp.2:5:
This verse says that the world of that time was destroyed by the flood, covered and lost beneath the waters. Peter refers to the flood in the days of Noah, although some scholars debate whether he speaks of the whole earth or of the human world of that time.

Peter writes to believers who were facing mockers. They said that Jesus would not come, because everything has stayed the same since the beginning. Peter answers that this is not true: God had already intervened in history with a massive judgment, and he did so through his word.

For today: do not let yourself be discouraged when it seems that nothing changes. God is patient, but he is also faithful. Live today with reverence, guard your heart, and trust that his promises will be fulfilled in their time.
exp.0:17:
It says that Peter and the other apostles personally heard the voice that came from heaven. They were with Jesus "on the holy mountain," that is, in a place where God was present in a special way.

Peter writes near the end of his life to strengthen believers who were hearing false teachers. He reminds them that his message is not based on invented stories, but on what he saw and heard. Many understand that he is referring to Jesus' transfiguration (Matthew 17), although the text does not name the mountain.

For today: our faith rests on real witnesses and on the Word of God. When doubts or strange ideas arise, return to what the Bible says about Jesus and let that testimony strengthen your heart.
exp.0:1:
It says that Peter wishes grace and peace to be multiplied for them, that is, that they grow more and more as they come to know God and Jesus our Lord better. The word translated "to you" points to the readers directly, and "multiplied" means "increased". Grace is the undeserved favor of God; peace is tranquility and harmony with Him.

Peter, an apostle of Jesus, writes to believers who received a faith as precious as that of the apostles. It is a greeting, but it also announces the theme of the letter: growing in the knowledge of God. The following verses explain that God has already given us everything necessary to live as He wants. Many understand that this "knowledge" is a personal relationship, not only information.

For today: spend a few minutes each day reading the Gospels and praying. In this way you will come to know Jesus better, and your trust and peace will grow little by little, even in difficult times.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that believers should make every effort to let their faith grow. To faith they must add "virtue," which here means moral strength and courage to do what is good. And to virtue, "knowledge" (the verse's word for understanding), that is, growing in understanding of what God is like and how he wants us to live. "Make every effort" means putting in the greatest effort.

Peter writes this letter to Christians in several regions, and he writes it near the end of his life. He has just reminded them that God has already given them everything needed to live in faith and godliness, along with great promises. For that reason he asks them for a response: to grow, not to stand still.

For today: do not assume your faith will grow on its own. Choose one concrete action this week, such as reading the Bible daily or practicing one good decision, and ask God for help to carry it out.
exp.0:3:
He says that God has given us precious and magnificent promises. Through them we can become partakers of the divine nature, that is, share in something of God's character, and so escape the corruption in the world caused by evil desires. The word "lust" in older translations corresponds here to evil desires, and the idea of escape describes a real change already underway. Christians understand this phrase in different ways, but it does not mean that we become gods.

Peter writes to believers and reminds them that God has already given them everything they need to live with faith and godliness. This verse is the foundation for what follows: since God has already acted, they must strive to grow in virtue, knowledge, and patience.

For today: when you feel drawn to desires that harm your life, remember God's promises. Read them, meditate on them, and ask Him for strength to live as He wants, trusting that He helps you to change.
exp.1:1:
This verse says that many will follow the depraved conduct of the false teachers. "Depravity" means behavior with no moral restraint, especially in sexual matters and the pursuit of pleasure. The way of truth will be defamed, that is, the gospel will be spoken of badly. Because of them, the Christian faith will be looked upon with disfavor.

The apostle Peter writes to believers and warns them with affection. Just as there were false prophets in Israel, there would also be false teachers within the church. Peter wants Christians to be alert and not to be led astray by those who teach one thing and live another.

For today: examine the one who teaches you, not only by what they say, but by how they live. And guard your own witness, because your conduct can draw others closer to Jesus or push them away.
exp.1:6:
It says God rescued Lot, whom Peter calls "righteous." Lot lived in Sodom and was deeply distressed by the depraved and lawless conduct of the people around him.

Peter writes to believers who face false teachers. To encourage them, he gives three examples: the flood, Sodom and Gomorrah, and the rescue of Lot. His point is that God knows how to punish the lawless and also how to rescue his own. Some wonder why he calls Lot righteous, since Genesis shows his failures. Peter seems to be speaking of his faith and of his distress at evil.

For today: if the wrongdoing around you hurts, that pain is not a lack of faith. Bring it to God, who knows your situation and knows how to rescue you.
exp.1:12:
Here Peter says that the false teachers will suffer the harm their wickedness has earned. The word "wages" here means what they have earned, and in this case it is a punishment. They consider it a pleasure to carouse in broad daylight. Peter calls them "blots and blemishes," that is, people who stain and shame the community. They feast together with the believers at their gatherings, yet they revel in their deception.

Peter writes to the churches to warn them about false teachers who slip in among them. He shows them that God judges those who teach lies and live without restraint, and that they should not be fooled by their religious appearance.

Today, it is not enough to simply be present in church or to share the table with other believers. Examine what teaching you listen to and compare it with the Bible. And review your own heart, so that your faith is not just outward appearance.
exp.0:10:
It says that if we live the way Peter describes, God will give us a lavish and generous welcome into the eternal kingdom of Jesus Christ. The words "lavish reception" are the part of the verse that points to this, so the reader can see it in the verse itself: the welcome is given, and it is given in full, with nothing held back.

Peter writes as an apostle, near the end of his life, to believers who already had faith. Earlier (vv. 5-8) he encouraged them to add to their faith virtue, knowledge, self-control, patience, godliness, brotherly affection, and love. Here he shows the result: a steady and purposeful life that does not waver.

For today: do not see spiritual growth as an optional extra. Choose one quality from the list, such as patience, and practice it this week with a concrete action. Do it trusting in the grace of Christ, not to earn your salvation.
exp.1:20:
It would be more serious to know the truth and then turn away from it than never to have known it at all. "The way of righteousness" means the life of faith and obedience that Christ teaches, and it is used here just as it appears in the verse. "Turn away" means to turn back from something once received, and "the holy commandment passed on to them" refers to the teaching of the gospel they received.

The apostle Peter speaks, warning believers about false teachers who promise freedom but live as slaves to their own desires. Peter describes people who came to know Christ but became entangled in sin again. Interpreters debate whether they were true believers or only sympathizers; the text does not fully settle this. What is clear is the seriousness of the warning.

For today: do not take lightly what God has shown you. If you feel yourself drifting away, do not wait; return to Him with humility, because His grace still invites you.
exp.0:9:
Peter urges believers to work harder at making their calling and election certain. "Calling" refers to God's call, and "election" means that God chose them. "Make sure" means to secure or confirm. He promises that if they practice these things, they will never stumble, that is, they will not fall away.

Peter writes near the end of his life to believers who already know the truth. "These things" are the qualities from the verses before: faith, goodness, knowledge, self-control, patience, godliness, brotherly kindness, and love. He wants their faith to be fruitful, not barren. God's call is secure, but a changed life confirms it before us.

Today, choose one of those qualities, such as patience or love for your brothers and sisters, and practice it this week through a concrete action. Ask God for His help. In this way your faith grows and becomes steadier.
exp.2:12:
This verse says that believers look forward to something better: new heavens and a new earth, just as God promised. What is special about that place is that righteousness dwells in it, meaning that what is right lives and reigns there, without wickedness or injustice. The word "dwells" means "lives."

Peter writes to Christians who had doubts because Jesus was not returning soon, and some were mocking that wait. He reminds them that God keeps what he promises, even though it happens in his own time. So he calls them to live holy lives while they wait. Christians understand the "new earth" in different ways, but all agree that God will make everything new.

For today: if we are waiting for a world where righteousness lives, we can start living that way now. Today you can choose to be honest, treat others with respect, and forgive, trusting that God will fulfill his promise.
exp.0:20:
No prophecy in the Bible was ever brought forth by a person's own will. Men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. The idea of being "carried along" is like a ship moved by the wind, guided by a force outside itself.

The apostle Peter, near the end of his life, speaks to believers who could be confused by false teachers. He wants them to trust Scripture more than opinions or invented stories. That is why he says prophecy does not depend on private interpretation, because its origin is God himself. Some understand that phrase in other ways, but the general meaning is clear.

For today: read the Bible with humility, asking the Spirit to teach you, and do not use it to justify your own ideas.
exp.1:18:
They promise freedom to others, yet they themselves are slaves to depravity. Peter's point is that whatever masters a person becomes the one who truly controls them. Those who claim to offer liberty are actually held captive by their own corrupt desires and destructive ways of living.

Peter, one of Jesus' apostles, writes to warn believers about false teachers who speak with impressive but empty words. They were promising freedom to live without moral limits, but Peter shows that this is not real freedom. He wants to protect the church from being deceived.

Today we can ask ourselves what habit, vice, or desire has us trapped while we believe we are free. Let us be wary of anyone who promises a life without consequences, and let us seek in Christ the true freedom, humbly admitting what dominates us and asking for help from God and from trusted brothers and sisters.
exp.0:13:
Peter says he knows his death is coming soon. He calls his body a "tent," something temporary that will be laid aside. He says that our Lord Jesus Christ has made this clear to him. The phrase "will soon be laid aside" means that his body will be set down at the end of his life.

Peter writes as an apostle near the end of his life, to believers who already know the truth. He wants to remind them of what matters most while he is still alive, so that they will not forget it after he is gone. Some think Jesus told him this when he spoke to him about his death, according to John 21:18-19, although the text does not make this clear.

For today: live with the awareness that life is short. Use your time to remember and pass on to others, with love and steadfastness, what is most important in your faith.
exp.0:15:
Peter says that what he and the other apostles taught about the power and coming of Jesus Christ was not made-up stories crafted to sound clever. They speak as eyewitnesses who saw the majesty of Jesus with their own eyes. "Power" means strength and authority, and "coming" refers to his arrival in glory. "Cleverly devised fables" are invented stories shaped with skill to persuade.

The apostle Peter writes near the end of his life, knowing that he will soon leave his body behind. He wants believers to hold onto the truth after his death. The verses that follow explain that he saw the glory of Jesus on the holy mountain, probably the transfiguration, and heard the voice of the Father.

Our faith does not rest on legends, but on the testimony of people who saw Jesus. Today you can read the Gospels with confidence and, when you have doubts, return to what those witnesses saw and wrote.
exp.0:19:
Peter says that the first thing we must understand is that no prophecy of Scripture comes from one's own interpretation. Some take this to mean how we read it ourselves; others take it to mean that the prophets did not produce the message on their own. The next verse supports this second idea.

Peter writes to believers near the end of his life. He has just reminded them that the prophetic word is a trustworthy light. He gives this warning because he will soon speak of false teachers who twist the truth.

For today: read the Bible with humility. Compare each passage with the rest of Scripture, ask the Holy Spirit for help, and also listen to other believers, instead of using a single verse to justify your own ideas.
exp.1:16:
This verse describes false teachers with two images. They are "springs without water": they promise to give life, but when you come near them there is nothing to drink. They are also "mists driven by a storm," that is, mist blown along by a strong wind that brings no rain. In the end, "blackest darkness" is reserved for them, a very strong expression that speaks of severe judgment.

The apostle Peter writes to believers to warn them against teachers who creep into the church. He compares them with Balaam, who loved unjust gain. These teachers speak with grand and attractive words, but they live enslaved to their own desires and draw others along with them.

For today: do not be swayed only by beautiful speeches or promises of freedom. Examine whether the teaching agrees with the Bible and whether the life of the one teaching bears good fruit.
exp.1:15:
It says that Balaam was corrected for his wickedness: a donkey, which cannot speak, spoke with a human voice and restrained the prophet's madness. The reader sees the verse with "was rebuked for his transgression" and "restrained." Here the word "transgression" means wrongdoing or going against what is right, and "restrained" means held back or stopped. The donkey is the animal that carries the load in this story.

Here the apostle Peter speaks, warning against false teachers inside the church. He compares them to Balaam, who according to Numbers 22 wanted to gain money by going against God's will. Peter uses that story to show that someone who is driven by greed can act foolishly, and that God is able to stop a person even through something as unexpected as a donkey.

For today: examine your motives, especially when it comes to money and success. If God corrects you through a person, a circumstance, or his Word, do not harden your heart. Listen with humility and change course in time.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that God, by his divine power, has already given us everything we need to live a life with God and to honor him. This comes through knowing Jesus, who called us by his own glory and excellence. "Godliness" means living with reverence toward God. "Excellence" here refers to moral goodness of character.

Peter, an apostle of Jesus, writes to believers who share the same precious faith. Before urging them to grow in character (vv. 5-7), he reminds them that God has already given them the resources. Many believe he writes to strengthen them against false teachers, something that appears later in the letter.

For today: when you feel weak or insufficient, remember that you do not start from zero. Spend time getting to know Jesus better through the Bible and prayer, and ask him to give you strength to obey him, trusting that his power sustains you.
exp.1:0:
This verse reminds us that, just as there were false prophets among the people of ancient Israel, there will also be false teachers among believers. They will secretly introduce destructive heresies, teachings that twist the truth and lead to ruin. They even deny the Master who bought them, that is, the one who paid for their freedom with his own life. In doing so, they bring swift destruction upon themselves.

The speaker is the apostle Peter, who writes to Christians and wants to guard them against deception. The verses that follow say that many will follow those teachers, that out of greed they will exploit people with false words, and that their judgment is not delayed. Some think he wrote shortly before his death; the Bible suggests this in chapter 1.

Today: compare what you hear with the Bible. Read the Scriptures yourself, and be wary of anyone who seeks your money or fame more than your spiritual good.
exp.0:12:
Peter says he thinks it is right to refresh his readers' memory about these things as long as he lives in the tent of his body. The word "tent" here means the body, a temporary dwelling rather than a permanent home. To refresh someone's memory means to encourage them or wake them up, and a reminder is a firm piece of advice that calls them back to what they already know.

The apostle Peter is speaking near the end of his life. He is writing to Christians who already know the truth, but he knows it is easy to forget. For that reason he insists on repeating the essentials, and in the next verse he says that his departure is near, as Jesus had shown him.

For today: do not grow tired of returning to the basics of the gospel. Even if you already know it, read it again, remind others of it with kindness, and thank those who repeat it to you. Faith stays firm when it is remembered every day.
exp.2:4:
This verse says that the mockers deliberately overlook something important: that long ago the heavens existed by the word of God, and the earth was formed out of water and by water. This means God brought the earth out of the water and kept it firmly established in the midst of it. "Deliberately" means this is not a lack of information, but that they choose not to see it.

The apostle Peter writes to believers to warn them about mockers who doubt the second coming of Christ. They say that everything has stayed the same since the beginning. Peter answers that God has already shown his power by his word, in creating the world and, as the text goes on, in sending the flood.

For today: when doubt or mockery troubles you, remember that the word of God has real power. That things seem the same does not mean God has forgotten his promises. Trust and wait with patience.

sum.0: Peter urges believers to grow in their faith, adding qualities such as self-control, patience, and love, because God has already given them everything they need along with great promises. Knowing that he will soon die, he reminds them of these things. He states that he saw the glory of Christ, and that Scripture comes from God through the Holy Spirit.
sum.1: Peter warns that false teachers will arise who will lead many people down paths of sin and greed, and that God will judge them, just as he judged the angels who sinned, the world in Noah's time, and Sodom and Gomorrah. He also teaches that God knows how to rescue his people. Turning back after coming to know Christ is worse than never having known him at all.
sum.2: Peter warns that in the last days scoffers will come who will doubt the promise of the Lord's return. He answers that God is patient, because he wants everyone to repent, even though his day will arrive suddenly. For this reason he calls believers to live holy lives, to wait for new heavens and a new earth, and to grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ.
